name: crowdos-mcp

tools.name: run_focus_group
tools.description:
Run a simulated focus group on a topic. Samples N AI agents from a demographic preset (e.g. us_general_population, gen_z, etc.), each with persistent Big Five personality + life context, and returns sentiment breakdown plus representative quotes. Synchronous — blocks 5-120s depending on population_size. Use this when you want quick public-opinion signal on a question, policy, product idea, or political stance.

RECOMMENDED FLOW (when the user is brief or didn't specify):
  1. If the user didn't pick an audience, call list_demographic_presets and propose 1-2 fitting presets.
  2. Call preview_cost with the proposed mode + population_size + num_rounds to get cents + seconds estimates.
  3. Confirm with the user: 'I'll run a 200-agent voting study on us_general_population (~$4.00, ~90s). Proceed?'
  4. Only then call run_focus_group.
If the user gave you explicit population_size + demographic_preset in their request, skip the confirmation step and run directly. Defaults are deliberately the Standard Pulse tier (200 agents) — that's the platform's balanced quality/cost call and what produces research-grade sentiment ratios. Plan panel caps: pro 750, max 2000 — on error_type=over_plan_cap, retry with the cap named in the error detail.

To target INSIDE a market (age band, cities, income — including real amounts in local currency — interests, ethnicity), pass custom_audience and preview it for free with estimate_reach first.

SAME PEOPLE ACROSS STEPS: persist_panel=true saves this run's respondents (result.panel.panel_id); pass that id as panel_id on later run_focus_group / run_debate / compare_options calls and omit population_size — the panel runs at its own size. panel_memory / evolve_panel are opt-in extras (see their descriptions).

Returns: { id, status, mode='voting', topic, demographic_preset, population_size, sentiment_summary: { positive, neutral, negative, positive_pct, neutral_pct, negative_pct } (counts + percentages, percentages sum to ~100), sample_responses: 5 agents each { agent_name, sentiment, reasoning, age, occupation }, total_responses, billing: { actual_cents, plan } }. Per-respondent quotes appear when the key has row-level results access; aggregate-level keys get the counts plus respondent_rows: 'aggregates-only…' instead of empty arrays. A panel run (persist_panel / panel_id) adds panel: { panel_id, size, preset_key, expires_at, [memory], [evolved_from] }. If you provided a stance_statement, an additional sentiment_axis field clarifies what positive/negative mean ('Agree' vs 'Disagree' instead of 'Positive' vs 'Negative'). Complete field-by-field reference for every result key: `GET https://api.crowdos.ai/api/v1/developer/docs`.

topic.description: The question or stance to test, e.g. 'Should the federal minimum wage be $20/hr?'

population_size.description: Number of agents to poll. Default 200 (Standard Pulse — research-grade sample). Plan caps: pro 750, max 2000.

demographic_preset.description: Audience preset. Use list_demographic_presets to see all options. Default: us_general_population.

stance_statement.description: Optional declarative the agents take a position FOR or AGAINST. Improves clarity on comparison questions.

language.description: ISO language code for agent responses. Default: en.

image_url.description: Optional public HTTPS URL of an image to attach to the question. One vision call extracts a description that every text-only agent reacts to alongside the question — useful for testing diagrams, product photos, charts, screenshots, or political imagery. Adds ~1-3s + ~$0.001 to the run regardless of population_size.

custom_audience.description: Optional filter narrowing the panel INSIDE the market preset. Keys (all optional): countries, regions, cities (each market's own vocabulary), age_min / age_max, genders ('all' | 'men' | 'women' | 'non_binary'), interests / interest_exclusions (taxonomy tags), income_min_tier / income_max_tier (affluence ladder 0-7, 7 = top), income_currency + income_min_amount / income_max_amount (REAL annual household amounts in a named ISO currency — currency is required with amounts; e.g. {'income_currency': 'USD', 'income_min_amount': 100000}), income_match ('position' = the equivalent affluence standing within each market's own income ladder, the default; 'absolute' = actual earnings at indicative FX), ethnicities / religions (multi-ethnic markets only). Preview a custom_audience with the free estimate_reach tool before paying for a run — it reports the audience size and which constraint cuts hardest. A 'small' audience is not a blocker: the panel is still delivered at the population_size you ask for, with every respondent matching the filter. Full field docs: `GET https://api.crowdos.ai/api/v1/developer/docs`.

persist_panel.description: Save this run's respondents as a reusable panel. The result carries panel: { panel_id, size, preset_key, created_at, expires_at } — quote panel_id back as `panel_id` on later runs so the SAME people answer every step (within-subjects testing: a difference between steps is then the stimulus, not the sample). Panels live 90 days; an account holds up to 200 (list_panels / delete_panel).

panel_id.description: Run against the SAME respondents as an earlier persist_panel run. The panel defines the audience wholesale — demographic_preset comes from it and custom_audience is refused — and it always runs at exactly its own size: omit population_size (the tool sends none), or pass the panel's size; any other value is a validation_error (panel_size_mismatch), a summoned panel is never subsampled. A missing, expired or foreign id is a 404 before billing. get_panel shows a panel's size and expiry; list_panels shows what the account has.

panel_memory.description: Opt-in panel memory, OFF by default. With persist_panel: the new panel records this session. With panel_id: each respondent recalls their OWN answers from up to the last 3 recorded sessions on that panel, and this session is recorded too; the result's panel.memory reports { recalled_members, recorded, members, sessions_kept }. Leave it off for step-by-step creative testing (a remembering panel carries order effects); turn it on for a tracker that revisits the same people over time.

evolve_panel.description: With panel_id only. Before the run, every respondent catches up on today's news for the panel's market (one reflection each) and the result is saved as a NEW panel whose parent_panel_id is the original — which stays frozen and replayable. The run uses the new panel; the result's panel block carries the new panel_id plus evolved_from and evolution: { headline_count, reflected, failed, evolved_at }. Included in the run's price.

tools.name: run_debate
tools.description:
Run a multi-round simulated debate. N agents discuss the topic across several rounds, updating their positions in response to peers. Returns final convergence (or lack of), key arguments, dissenting views, and a synthesis. Use this when you want to see whether a position survives scrutiny or how disagreement evolves, not just a snapshot poll.

RECOMMENDED FLOW: same as run_focus_group — for non-trivial studies, call list_demographic_presets (if the user didn't pick an audience), then preview_cost (debates run population_size × num_rounds LLM calls so cost climbs fast), then confirm with the user before firing. Defaults match the platform's standard debate (30 agents × 5 rounds) — that's the calibrated quality bar; smaller debates produce noisier convergence scores. The default fits every plan's panel cap. custom_audience narrows who debates — preview it with estimate_reach. panel_id runs the debate on a panel saved by an earlier persist_panel run (omit population_size — the panel runs at its own size).

Returns: final_consensus_score (0-1; higher = more aligned), summary (synthesis paragraph), key_arguments_for / key_arguments_against (string arrays), dissenting_views (string array of holdout positions), final_round_responses (up to 5 agents from the LAST round only — each with agent_name, position, reasoning, confidence), num_rounds, agent_count, position_shifts_count (how many position changes happened across the debate); a panel run adds panel: { panel_id, … }.

topic.description: The motion the panel debates, e.g. 'Should the federal minimum wage be $20/hr?'

num_rounds.description: Debate rounds. Default 5 (platform standard). More rounds = more convergence pressure and cleaner consensus, but cost grows linearly.

population_size.description: Number of agents in the debate. Default 30 (platform standard — calibrated quality). Cost = population_size × num_rounds LLM calls.

demographic_preset.description: Audience preset. Use list_demographic_presets to see all options. Default: us_general_population.

stance_statement.description: Optional declarative the agents argue FOR or AGAINST. Sharpens the split when the topic is open-ended.

image_url.description: Optional public HTTPS URL of an image to attach to the debate topic. Same shape as run_focus_group.image_url.

tools.name: compare_options
tools.description:
Run a simulated A/B (or A/B/C/…) test on 2-10 text options (plan limits: pro 5, max 10 — above your plan's limit the call returns over_plan_cap). Each agent reads all options and ranks them; you get a leaderboard with Borda counts, the winning option, and sample reasoning. Use for product descriptions, ad headlines, policy framings, slogans, value props — any case where you want to know 'which of these resonates best with X audience'.

Synchronous — blocks 5-90s depending on population_size. Cost is ~25% higher than the same-size voting study (prompt carries all options).

RECOMMENDED FLOW: same as run_focus_group — call list_demographic_presets if audience unclear, preview_cost for budget, confirm with user, then run. To have the SAME people rank several rounds of options, save the panel once (persist_panel) and pass its panel_id afterwards, omitting population_size.

Returns: { id, status, mode='comparison', topic, demographic_preset, population_size, options: [{id, label, text}], winner: option_id, leaderboard: ranked rows with borda_score / borda_pct / first_place_votes, sample_responses: 5 agents each { agent_name, top_pick, conviction (0-1), one_liner, top_rankings: 2 entries with reasoning }, total_responses, billing, [panel] }. Quotes appear when the key has row-level results access; aggregate-level keys get respondent_rows: 'aggregates-only…' instead.

topic.description: The question framing the comparison, e.g. 'Which of these product descriptions resonates most with you?'

options.description: 2-10 text options to compare. Each option is a string up to 500 chars (a full product description / ad headline / policy framing). Plan limits: pro 5, max 10 — more than your plan allows returns over_plan_cap.

tools.name: test_pricing
tools.description:
Run a classic quantitative pricing study on the simulated panel. Two instruments:

  van_westendorp — the Price Sensitivity Meter. Each respondent gives four prices (too cheap / bargain / getting expensive / too expensive). Returns the four standard crossing points: OPP (optimal price point), IPP (indifference price point), and the PMC-PME acceptable range. Use when you do NOT yet have a price in mind and want the range the market will bear.

  gabor_granger — you supply a price ladder; each respondent states the highest rung they'd still buy at. Returns a demand curve, a revenue curve, and the revenue-maximising rung. Use when you already have candidate price points and want to pick between them.

Bills at the standard voting per-agent rate — a pricing study costs the same as a focus group of the same size. Call preview_cost with mode='voting' for an estimate.

Returns: { id, status, mode='pricing', instrument_type, topic, demographic_preset, population_size, respondents_analyzed, sample_responses[0..5], billing, and then per instrument — van_westendorp: price_points { optimal_price_point, indifference_price_point, point_of_marginal_cheapness, point_of_marginal_expensiveness, acceptable_range } + excluded_non_monotonic; gabor_granger: revenue_maximizing_price + demand_curve + revenue_curve + price_ladder + warnings[] }.

Note on a null revenue_maximizing_price: when no respondent would buy at any rung of the ladder there is no revenue-maximising price, so it comes back null and warnings[] says so. The ladder probably sits above what this audience will pay; try lower rungs.

Note on excluded_non_monotonic: Van Westendorp respondents whose four prices aren't in ascending order are excluded from the curves — standard PSM practice, and the same thing a human panel does. They are still counted in the panel and still billed, because they did answer. Report respondents_analyzed, not population_size, as the base for the price points.

product.description: What is being priced. Be concrete — respondents answer with real money, so 'a 12-week online course in conversational Spanish, 2 live classes a week' produces far better numbers than 'a language course'.

instrument.description: van_westendorp to discover an acceptable range; gabor_granger to choose among prices you already have. gabor_granger requires `ladder`.

ladder.description: Gabor-Granger only: 2-20 candidate prices, e.g. [9.99, 14.99, 19.99, 24.99]. Ignored for van_westendorp.

currency.description: Currency symbol shown to respondents. Default '$'.

market_context.description: Optional one-line anchor, e.g. 'competitors charge $15-25/month'. Supply it only if it is true — it moves the answers.

population_size.description: Respondents. Default 200. Van Westendorp drops non-monotonic answers, so the analyzed base is typically 10-25% below this — size up if you need a specific analyzed n.

demographic_preset.description: Audience preset. Use list_demographic_presets. Default: us_general_population.

tools.name: rank_items
tools.description:
Rank a long list of items — messages, claims, features, reasons to buy, decision criteria, buying occasions — by best-worst scaling (MaxDiff) on the simulated panel. Each respondent sees a few small sets drawn from the list and names the MOST and LEAST in each; the panel as a whole covers the full list. Use it to shortlist 15-25 out of up to 200 candidates before real fieldwork, or to order a shorter list by what matters.

Why this and not compare_options: compare_options ranks 2-10 options that every respondent sees together. rank_items handles 4-200, and because every judgment is relative (most vs least within a set) the result is a rank order rather than a level — the part a simulated panel is strongest at.

Bills at the standard voting per-agent rate. Call preview_cost with mode='voting' for an estimate. A 200-respondent panel gives stable ranks for lists up to about 60 items; use 400+ for 100-200 items.

Returns: { id, status, mode='maxdiff', instrument_type, topic, demographic_preset, population_size, respondents_analyzed, screens_answered, question, ranking[ {rank, item, bw_score, share_pct, rank_ci95, p_top5, best, worst, appearances} ], adjacent_separation[ {rank, vs_rank, p_higher} ], appearances {min, mean, max}, warnings[], reading_guide, sample_responses[0..5], billing }.

Read it as an ORDER. bw_score is (best minus worst) divided by appearances, in [-1, 1]; share_pct is that score rescaled to sum to 100 for communication — not a population percentage. rank_ci95 is a bootstrap interval over respondents; treat items whose intervals overlap as tied. adjacent_separation gives how often rank k stayed above rank k+1 across the bootstrap — the answer to 'can this panel tell #1 from #2'. warnings names items that appeared too few times to rank reliably; raise population_size or screens_per_agent.

topic.description: What the items are about — the context respondents judge them in, e.g. 'reasons to switch mobile carrier' or 'front-of-pack claims for a new oat milk'. Required.

items.description: 4-200 short texts to rank, one item each. Duplicates are merged.

question.description: The criterion asked on every set, phrased as a most/least question. Default: 'Which ONE of these matters MOST to you, and which ONE matters LEAST?'

screens_per_agent.description: Sets each respondent answers. Default: enough to see the list about once, capped at 12 — past that, coverage comes from panel size, not longer prompts.

population_size.description: Respondents. Default 200. Each item needs to be shown many times across the panel for a stable rank — size up for long lists.

demographic_preset.description: Audience preset. Use list_demographic_presets. Default: us_general_population.

tools.name: pretest_questions
tools.description:
Pretest draft survey questions on the simulated panel BEFORE fielding them for real. Each respondent is shown a subset of your questions and, for each one, restates it in their own words, answers it, and flags what is wrong with it (double-barrelled, ambiguous, leading, no option that fits, too long). A deterministic wording check runs on all of them in addition. Every question comes back with a verdict: ok, check, or revise.

Use it as a gate, not a study: run it on a draft item bank, fix or drop everything marked revise, then field the survey for real. It is the cheapest step in a research pipeline and catches the errors that silently ruin a real one — a question half the panel reads differently than you wrote it, or an option list with no honest answer in it.

Bills at the standard voting per-agent rate; a pretest needs far fewer respondents than a study. 50 is usually enough — each question needs a few dozen readers, not a representative sample. Call preview_cost with mode='voting' for an estimate.

Returns: { id, status, mode='pretest', instrument_type, topic, demographic_preset, population_size, respondents_analyzed, summary {revise, check, ok}, items[ {id, text, respondents, verdict, flag_rates {double_barreled, ambiguous, leading, missing_option, too_long}, clean_pct, panel_flags, paraphrase_consistency, option_distribution, none_fit_pct, dominant_option_pct, rule_hits[], restated_samples, notes} ], warnings[], reading_guide, billing }.

Read it as a VERDICT LIST, not a finding. paraphrase_consistency is how much respondents' restatements agree with each other — low means the question is being read more than one way, which is the single most useful signal here. option_distribution and none_fit_pct are a floor/ceiling check on your draft options (everyone picking the same option, or none of them) — never quote them as a result. rule_hits are deterministic wording faults found without the panel.

topic.description: What the questionnaire is about — the context respondents read the questions in, e.g. 'a survey about grocery delivery habits'. Required.

items.description: 1-40 draft questions. A plain string is an open-ended question; use {text, options, id} to pretest a closed question with its answer list (up to 12 options) and keep your own id on the result. Duplicates are merged.

items_per_agent.description: Questions each respondent is shown. Default: the whole bank, capped at 10 — past that, coverage comes from panel size, not longer prompts.

population_size.description: Respondents. Default 50. Each question needs a few dozen readers for the flag rates to mean anything; size up when the bank is large enough that each respondent sees only part of it.

demographic_preset.description: Audience preset — pretest on the audience you will actually field to, since readability depends on who is reading. Use list_demographic_presets. Default: us_general_population.

custom_audience.description: Optional filter narrowing the panel INSIDE the market preset. Keys (all optional): countries, regions, cities (each market's own vocabulary), age_min / age_max, genders ('all' | 'men' | 'women' | 'non_binary'), interests / interest_exclusions (taxonomy tags), income_min_tier / income_max_tier (affluence ladder 0-7, 7 = top), income_currency + income_min_amount / income_max_amount (REAL annual household amounts in a named ISO currency — currency is required with amounts; e.g. {'income_currency': 'USD', 'income_min_amount': 100000}), income_match ('position' = the equivalent affluence standing within each market's own income ladder, the default; 'absolute' = actual earnings at indicative FX), ethnicities / religions (multi-ethnic markets only). Preview a custom_audience with the free estimate_reach tool before paying for a run — it reports the audience size and which constraint cuts hardest. A 'small' audience is not a blocker: the panel is still delivered at the population_size you ask for, with every respondent matching the filter. Full field docs: `GET https://api.crowdos.ai/api/v1/developer/docs`.

persist_panel.description: Save this run's respondents as a reusable panel. The result carries panel: { panel_id, size, preset_key, created_at, expires_at } — quote panel_id back as `panel_id` on later runs so the SAME people answer every step (within-subjects testing: a difference between steps is then the stimulus, not the sample). Panels live 90 days; an account holds up to 200 (list_panels / delete_panel).

panel_id.description: Run against the SAME respondents as an earlier persist_panel run. The panel defines the audience wholesale — demographic_preset comes from it and custom_audience is refused — and it always runs at exactly its own size: omit population_size (the tool sends none), or pass the panel's size; any other value is a validation_error (panel_size_mismatch), a summoned panel is never subsampled. A missing, expired or foreign id is a 404 before billing. get_panel shows a panel's size and expiry; list_panels shows what the account has.

panel_memory.description: Opt-in panel memory, OFF by default. With persist_panel: the new panel records this session. With panel_id: each respondent recalls their OWN answers from up to the last 3 recorded sessions on that panel, and this session is recorded too; the result's panel.memory reports { recalled_members, recorded, members, sessions_kept }. Leave it off for step-by-step creative testing (a remembering panel carries order effects); turn it on for a tracker that revisits the same people over time.

evolve_panel.description: With panel_id only. Before the run, every respondent catches up on today's news for the panel's market (one reflection each) and the result is saved as a NEW panel whose parent_panel_id is the original — which stays frozen and replayable. The run uses the new panel; the result's panel block carries the new panel_id plus evolved_from and evolution: { headline_count, reflected, failed, evolved_at }. Included in the run's price.

tools.name: list_demographic_presets
tools.description:
List all available demographic presets (audience templates). Each preset is a calibrated mix of demographics + Big Five OCEAN personality distributions for a country, region, or behavioral segment. Call this first if you don't know which preset to use.

Returns: { presets: [ { key, label, description, age_range } ] }. Pass the `key` to run_focus_group / run_debate as demographic_preset.

tools.name: get_simulation
tools.description:
Fetch the FULL results of a previously-run simulation by id. Use when run_focus_group's trimmed response isn't enough and you need every agent response.

ALSO USE THIS to recover a run whose tool call failed after the study launched — if any run tool returns error='stream_disconnected' or 'timeout', or any error carrying recoverable: true, the simulation is still running (or has already finished) on the server and the error's sim_id field names it. Do NOT re-run the tool — that launches and bills a second study. Wait 30-60 seconds, then call get_simulation(sim_id). If status is 'running', poll again. If status is 'complete', you have your result. If status is 'cancelled' / 'failed', the sim ended without a result.

Returns the same shape as the originating run tool but without the 5-quote cap — every agent's response is included when the key has row-level results access (aggregate-level keys get respondent_rows: 'aggregates-only…'). A test_pricing / rank_items / pretest_questions run returns its headline fields (price points, ranking or verdicts) plus the complete analysis block as `analysis`. Internal QA fields (consistency_score, model routing, harness flags) are still stripped to keep context manageable. Voting responses carry agent_name + sentiment + reasoning + age + occupation; debate rounds carry agent_name + position + reasoning + confidence. Also includes top-level `status` (running | complete | failed | cancelled) so you can poll in-flight sims.

sim_id.description: The id returned by any run tool, OR the sim_id field of a run tool's error (stream_disconnected, timeout, or any error carrying recoverable: true).

tools.name: cancel_simulation
tools.description:
Explicitly cancel a running simulation and refund the wallet reservation. Use when:
  - The user changes their mind mid-run
  - You realize the parameters were wrong (e.g., wrong     audience, typo in topic)
  - A long-running debate is going off the rails

Closing the MCP session does NOT cancel the simulation — the run continues server-side and results land in the DB. Only call this if you genuinely want to stop the run AND refund the cents. Returns 409 if the sim is already terminal.

sim_id.description: The id of the running simulation.

tools.name: crowd_sample
tools.description:
Browse the persistent CrowdOS crowd — a sample of the live agent population, sanitized to remove internal IDs. Useful for showing 'what kind of people are in this audience' to a user. No API key required — this endpoint is public.

Returns: { total_population, sample_size, agents: [ { name, age, gender, occupation, country, ocean: { openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism }, values, media_diet, political_ideology, latest_opinion, recent_headline } ] }.

limit.description: How many agents to sample, 1-100. Default: 20.

tools.name: list_panels
tools.description:
List the saved panels on this account — the rosters persist_panel and evolve_panel runs created — newest first, metadata only (never the respondents). Free. Use it to find the panel_id for a follow-up run, to see which panels are near expiry, or to check the 200-live-panel ceiling before another persist_panel.

Returns: { panels: [ { panel_id, size, preset_key, created_at, expires_at, last_used_at, use_count, source_sim_id (the run that created it), parent_panel_id (set when the panel was evolved from another), evolved_at, session_count (sessions recorded by panel_memory runs) } ], count, limit, offset, live_limit }. Expired panels are not listed — they are gone.

limit.description: Panels per page (max 200 = the live-panel ceiling, so one page always fits everything).

offset.description: Rows to skip for paging. Default: 0.

tools.name: get_panel
tools.description:
Metadata and demographic make-up of one saved panel you own — never the roster. Free. Check a panel's size and expires_at before summoning it with panel_id, or audit who is inside it: by_dimension carries head-counts by age band, gender, region and income band (the same keys estimate_reach reports), and sessions lists what panel_memory runs asked and when (never the answers).

Returns: { panel_id, size, preset_key, created_at, expires_at, last_used_at, use_count, source_sim_id, parent_panel_id, evolved_at, session_count, sessions: [ { sim_id, topic, mode, recorded_at } ], by_dimension }. A missing, expired or foreign panel_id is a not-found error.

panel_id.description: The panel_id from a persist_panel result or list_panels.

tools.name: delete_panel
tools.description:
Delete a saved panel you own — immediate and permanent. A run already in flight on it is unaffected; a run launched afterwards with that panel_id gets a not-found error before billing. Deleting a parent leaves the panels evolved from it in place. Accounts hold up to 200 live panels — delete to make room. Confirm with the user before deleting a panel they may still want to summon.

Returns: { panel_id, deleted: true }.

panel_id.description: The panel_id to delete, from a persist_panel result or list_panels. Immediate and permanent.

tools.name: estimate_reach
tools.description:
Preview how broad an audience a custom_audience filter describes — FREE: no model calls, no wallet debit, returns in under a second. Call it before a run that uses custom_audience to check the spec is valid and to see how tight the cut is.

A small audience is NOT a blocked one. Every panel is delivered at the population_size you request, with every respondent satisfying your filter. So never refuse or abandon a run because this returns audience_size 'small' — run it, and tell the user the audience is narrow. The band tells you how much natural variety sits behind the panel: a very small audience's results carry an audience_note saying they reflect a narrower range of perspectives, which is a reason to suggest widening the filter, not to stop.

Returns: { audience_size ('small' | 'medium' | 'large'), narrowed_by (the single filter cutting hardest — age, gender, geo, income, ethnicity, religion, interests or exclusions; null if nothing is narrowing it), narrowing_filters (every narrowing filter, strongest first; narrowed_by is its first entry), preset_key, and — with include_by_dimension=true — by_dimension as percentage shares }.

Note on interests: respondents each carry a handful of tags from a ~200-topic taxonomy, so ANY single tag describes only a small slice of a market. Pass several related tags (they are OR-matched) when you want a broader cut — e.g. 'Stock Trading' plus 'Day Trading' and 'Personal Investing' rather than 'Stock Trading' alone.

The market is preset_key; demographic_preset, the name the run tools use, is accepted too (both at once must name the same market).

An impossible spec (unknown country, gender, heritage value, currency code or income_match; an interest that is not a taxonomy tag; a city or region the market does not have; an unknown market; a heritage cut on a market without that axis; an income range no band on the market's ladder falls inside) returns audience_size=null plus spec_errors (human strings) and spec_error_details [{code, field, values, allowed, message}] — the same stable codes a run would reject with (422, before any charge) — so fix the spec here, for free.

targeting.description: Optional filter narrowing the panel INSIDE the market preset. Keys (all optional): countries, regions, cities (each market's own vocabulary), age_min / age_max, genders ('all' | 'men' | 'women' | 'non_binary'), interests / interest_exclusions (taxonomy tags), income_min_tier / income_max_tier (affluence ladder 0-7, 7 = top), income_currency + income_min_amount / income_max_amount (REAL annual household amounts in a named ISO currency — currency is required with amounts; e.g. {'income_currency': 'USD', 'income_min_amount': 100000}), income_match ('position' = the equivalent affluence standing within each market's own income ladder, the default; 'absolute' = actual earnings at indicative FX), ethnicities / religions (multi-ethnic markets only). Preview a custom_audience with the free estimate_reach tool before paying for a run — it reports the audience size and which constraint cuts hardest. A 'small' audience is not a blocker: the panel is still delivered at the population_size you ask for, with every respondent matching the filter. Full field docs: `GET https://api.crowdos.ai/api/v1/developer/docs`.

preset_key.description: Market preset to sample. Use list_demographic_presets for the roster. Default: us_general_population.

demographic_preset.description: The same market under the name the run tools use. Send this or preset_key; if both are sent they must name the same market.

sample_size.description: How much evidence the size band rests on. Default 500. Snapped up to the nearest of 100/250/500/1000/2500/5000/10000. An input only — it is not echoed in the response.

include_by_dimension.description: Also return the matched sample's composition by age band / gender / region / income.

tools.name: preview_cost
tools.description:
Estimate the cost (cents) and runtime (seconds) of a hypothetical run_focus_group or run_debate call WITHOUT actually running it. Use this when you need to budget before committing — autonomous agents should preview before any sim with population_size > 100 or any debate at all.

Free to call (no wallet debit, no rate-limit penalty beyond the regular per-key limit). Pricing is a fixed rate per respondent. Returns: estimate_cents (what a real run reserves — a completed vote is charged exactly this), min_cents / max_cents (the settle range: a debate may settle lower if it reaches consensus early, down to min_cents; respondents who fail to answer are never charged), expected_seconds_min / expected_seconds_max (so you can set a sensible tool-call timeout), plan, agent_cap, and within_agent_cap (false means the population_size exceeds the user's plan limit and the real call would 400).

mode.description: Which study to price: voting (one pass) or debate (priced per round). Default: voting.

population_size.description: Default 200 to match run_focus_group's Standard Pulse default. Pass the same value the user agreed to.

num_rounds.description: Debate-only. Default 5 to match run_debate's platform-standard default. Ignored for voting.

instructions: CrowdOS runs simulated focus groups, debates, A/B tests and pricing studies against census-grounded panels. Recommended flow: list_demographic_presets to pick a market, estimate_reach (free) when using custom_audience, preview_cost to budget, then the run tool. Runs debit the account's wallet — confirm cost with the user before large panels. To put the SAME respondents through several steps, run once with persist_panel=true and pass the returned panel_id to later runs (omit population_size); list_panels / get_panel / delete_panel manage saved panels. Full written reference: GET /api/v1/developer/docs on this host.
